# Categorical predictors

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Categorical predictors";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` mantis shrimp have [12]{.hl} types of photoreceptor for colour in their eyes. Humans have three.

_Source: Thoen et al. (2014), Science_
:::

## Today

- What a categorical predictor is, and how R stores it: factors
- Treatment coding: the default in R
- Dummy coding by hand, and changing the reference level
- Sum coding
- Predictors with more than two levels
- Combining categorical and continuous predictors

## So far

Until now every predictor was a number: frequency, length, body mass. Each slope was a change in `y` per unit of `x`.

. . .

Many linguistic predictors are categories instead: voicing (voiced, voiceless), speaking style (casual, clear, loud), language, condition, speaker group, word class.

. . .

What does "one unit more" mean for `voicing`?

## The data

Vowels are longer before [voiced]{.hl} consonants (_bead_) than before [voiceless]{.hl} ones (_beat_). A simulated production study:

```{r}
set.seed(7)
vowels <- tibble(
  voicing  = rep(c("voiceless", "voiced"), each = 60),
  duration = round(c(rnorm(60, 120, 20), rnorm(60, 160, 22)))   # ms
)
vowels |> summarise(mean = mean(duration), sd = sd(duration), n = n(), .by = voicing)
```

## The data

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.4}
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = voicing, y = duration, colour = voicing)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 6, shape = 18, colour = mist) +
  labs(x = "Following consonant", y = "Vowel duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

White: the mean of each group. A model with voicing as a predictor should recover these two means.

# Treatment coding

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` mantis shrimp come in two kinds: [smashers]{.hl} break open crabs, clams and snails with club-like limbs, and spearers ambush fish from their burrows and impale them.

_Source: UC Berkeley News_
:::

## `lm()` with a categorical predictor {.smaller}

```{r}
m <- lm(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels)
coef(m)
```

. . .

Compare with the group means:

```{r}
vowels |> summarise(mean = mean(duration), .by = voicing)
```

. . .

- The __intercept__ is the mean of `voiced`
- The __slope__ `voicingvoiceless` is the difference: voiceless minus voiced

## The reference level

Why is `voiced` the intercept?

. . .

R turns text into a `factor`, and puts its levels in alphabetical order:

```{r}
levels(factor(vowels$voicing))
```

. . .

The first level becomes the __reference level__. Every other level is compared against it.

. . .

R names the coefficient `voicingvoiceless`: the predictor, then the level being compared with the reference.

## Treatment coding, visually

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
means <- vowels |> summarise(duration = mean(duration), .by = voicing) |>
  mutate(x = if_else(voicing == "voiced", 0, 1))

vowels |>
  mutate(x = if_else(voicing == "voiced", 0, 1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = duration)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = voicing), width = 0.06, alpha = 0.4, size = 2) +
  geom_line(data = means, colour = mist, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = means, colour = mist, size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.08, y = means$duration[means$x == 0] + 6, hjust = 0, colour = mist, size = 5,
           label = "intercept = mean of voiced") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.55, y = mean(means$duration) + 8, hjust = 0, colour = hornbill, size = 5,
           label = paste("slope =", round(diff(rev(means$duration)), 1), "ms")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1), labels = c("voiced\n(0)", "voiceless\n(1)"),
                     limits = c(-0.25, 1.25)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Vowel duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Code the reference level as 0 and the other as 1: the regression line goes through the two means. A one-unit change in x is the change from one category to the other.

## Dummy coding by hand

This is exactly what R does behind the scenes:

```{r}
vowels <- vowels |>
  mutate(voiceless01 = if_else(voicing == "voiceless", 1, 0))

coef(lm(duration ~ voiceless01, data = vowels))
```

. . .

Same numbers as before. A variable coded 0 and 1 like this is called a __dummy variable__.

## Changing the reference level {.smaller}

Voiceless is the more natural baseline here. Set the order of the levels with `fct_relevel()` from `{forcats}`:

```{r}
vowels <- vowels |>
  mutate(voicing = fct_relevel(voicing, "voiceless"))

levels(vowels$voicing)
coef(lm(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels))
```

. . .

The intercept is now the `voiceless` mean, and the slope is +`r round(diff(tapply(vowels$duration, vowels$voicing, mean)))` ms for voiced. The model and its fit are unchanged; only the comparison is different.

## Choosing the reference level

- Choose the level that makes the coefficients easiest to read, often a natural baseline: a control condition, the standard variety, the most frequent category
- Set it explicitly, rather than relying on the alphabet

. . .

In R, the reference level of a factor is simply its first level.

## Discussion

Your study compares L1 English speakers with three groups of L2 speakers of English, whose first languages are German, Italian and Mandarin.

- Which group would you choose as the reference level, and why?
- Would your choice change if your question were about differences among the three L2 groups?

# Sum coding

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the peacock mantis shrimp strikes snail shells at up to [23 m/s]{.hl} (about 83 km/h), with accelerations of up to 8,000 times gravity. The strike also makes bubbles that collapse with destructive force.

_Sources: Patek, Korff & Caldwell (2004), Nature; UC Berkeley News_
:::

## Sum coding

Instead of 0 and 1, code the two levels as +1 and −1:

```{r}
contrasts(vowels$voicing) <- contr.sum(2)
contrasts(vowels$voicing)
```

. . .

```{r}
coef(lm(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels))
```

## Reading sum-coded coefficients

```{r}
means <- vowels |> summarise(mean = mean(duration), .by = voicing)
mean(means$mean)                      # the mean of the group means
diff(means$mean) / 2                  # half the difference
```

. . .

- The __intercept__ is the [grand mean]{.hl}: the average of the group means
- The __coefficient__ is how far each group lies from that grand mean: `+` for the first level, `−` for the second

## Sum coding, visually

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
grand <- mean(means$mean)
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = voicing, y = duration, colour = voicing)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.4, size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = grand, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(data = means, aes(x = voicing, xend = voicing, y = grand, yend = mean),
               colour = mist, linewidth = 1.2,
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"))) +
  geom_point(data = means, aes(y = mean), colour = mist, size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = grand + 4, label = "grand mean = intercept",
           colour = mist, size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Following consonant", y = "Vowel duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Arrows: the sum-coded coefficient, `±` `r round(abs(diff(means$mean)) / 2, 1)` ms from the grand mean.

## Treatment or sum coding?

| | Treatment (0 / 1) | Sum (+1 / −1) |
|---|---|---|
| Intercept | mean of the reference level | [grand mean]{.hl} |
| Coefficient | difference from the reference | deviation from the grand mean |
| Default in R | yes | no: `contr.sum()` |

. . .

The fit is identical. The choice changes what the intercept means, which matters most when you add interactions (next week).

# More than two levels

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` despite their 12 receptors, mantis shrimp were [worse]{.hl} than humans, bees and butterflies at telling similar colours apart. They seem to encode colour unlike any other animal studied: perhaps by recognising colours rather than comparing them.

_Sources: Thoen et al. (2014), Science; Sci.News_
:::

## Speaking style

A simulated study of vowel duration in three speaking styles:

```{r}
set.seed(9)
styles <- tibble(
  style    = rep(c("casual", "clear", "loud"), each = 50),
  duration = round(c(rnorm(50, 110, 18), rnorm(50, 150, 20), rnorm(50, 132, 19)))
)
styles |> summarise(mean = mean(duration), .by = style)
```

## Speaking style

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.4}
ggplot(styles, aes(x = style, y = duration, colour = style)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 6, shape = 18, colour = mist) +
  labs(x = "Speaking style", y = "Vowel duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Three levels, two coefficients

```{r}
m_style <- lm(duration ~ style, data = styles)
coef(m_style)
```

. . .

The intercept is the mean of `casual`, the reference level. `styleclear` is clear minus casual, and `styleloud` is loud minus casual.

. . .

A predictor with `k` levels gets `k − 1` coefficients: each level against the reference.

## Three levels, visually

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.0}
style_means <- styles |> summarise(mean = mean(duration), .by = style)
casual_mean <- style_means$mean[style_means$style == "casual"]
ggplot(styles, aes(x = style, y = duration, colour = style)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.35, size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = casual_mean, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(data = filter(style_means, style != "casual"),
               aes(x = style, xend = style, y = casual_mean, yend = mean),
               colour = mist, linewidth = 1.2, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"))) +
  geom_point(data = style_means, aes(y = mean), colour = mist, size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = casual_mean - 6, label = "intercept", colour = mist, hjust = 0, size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Speaking style", y = "Vowel duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Each arrow is one coefficient: how far clear and loud speech lie from casual speech, the dashed line.

## Behind the scenes {.smaller}

R creates one dummy variable per non-reference level:

```{r}
model.matrix(~ style, data = styles)[c(1, 51, 101), ]
```

. . .

| style | styleclear | styleloud | predicted duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| casual | 0 | 0 | b₀ |
| clear | 1 | 0 | b₀ + b₁ |
| loud | 0 | 1 | b₀ + b₂ |

## What is missing?

The model does not directly compare `clear` with `loud`.

. . .

Change the reference level to get that comparison:

```{r}
styles |>
  mutate(style = fct_relevel(style, "clear")) |>
  lm(duration ~ style, data = _) |>
  coef()
```

. . .

`data = _` uses the native pipe's placeholder: the data come from the pipe.

## Sum coding with three levels

```{r}
styles <- styles |> mutate(style = factor(style))
contrasts(styles$style) <- contr.sum(3)
coef(lm(duration ~ style, data = styles))
```

. . .

The intercept is now the [grand mean]{.hl} of the three styles. `style1` is casual's deviation from it and `style2` is clear's. Loud's deviation is not shown, because it is minus the sum of the other two.

## Model fit and assumptions {.smaller}

```{r}
glance(m_style)[, 1:2]
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.2}
augment(m_style) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = style, y = .resid, colour = style)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The same assumptions as before. With categories, check that the residuals have a similar spread in every group.

# Mixing predictors

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` mantis shrimp were the first animals shown to see [circularly polarised]{.hl} light. Some species also reflect it from body parts they display in courtship.

_Source: Chiou et al. (2008), Current Biology_
:::

## Categorical and continuous together

Back to the warning from lecture 4: bill length by bill depth.

```{r}
bills <- drop_na(penguins, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)
coef(lm(bill_length_mm ~ bill_depth_mm, data = bills))
```

. . .

Add `species` as a second predictor:

```{r}
m_bills <- lm(bill_length_mm ~ bill_depth_mm + species, data = bills)
coef(m_bills)
```

. . .

With species in the model, the bill depth slope turns positive, as it is within each species.

## Three parallel lines

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
bills_fit <- augment(m_bills)
ggplot(bills_fit, aes(x = bill_depth_mm, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = bill_length_mm), alpha = 0.45, size = 2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted), linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Bill depth (mm)", y = "Bill length (mm)", colour = NULL)
```

One slope for bill depth, and a different intercept for each species (Adelie is the reference). The lines are parallel: no interaction.

## Reading the mixed model

```{r}
tidy(m_bills)[, 1:2]
```

. . .

| Coefficient | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `bill_depth_mm` | `r round(coef(m_bills)["bill_depth_mm"], 2)` mm of length per mm of depth, within a species |
| `speciesChinstrap` | Chinstrap bills are `r round(coef(m_bills)["speciesChinstrap"], 1)` mm longer than Adelie bills of the same depth |
| `speciesGentoo` | Gentoo bills, `r round(coef(m_bills)["speciesGentoo"], 1)` mm longer |

## Other coding schemes

Treatment and sum coding are the two you will meet most. There are others, for example:

- [Helmert]{.hl} coding: each level against the mean of the previous levels
- [Successive differences]{.hl}: each level against the previous one, for ordered categories

. . .

All of them give the same fit. They differ only in which comparisons the coefficients show: choose the one that matches your research question.

# Your turn

## Exercises

With `penguins`:

1. Model `body_mass_g` by `species`. Check that the coefficients match the group means.
2. Make `Gentoo` the reference level and refit. What changed?
3. Refit with sum coding. What is the intercept now?
4. Model `body_mass_g` by `sex` and `flipper_length_mm` together. Interpret both coefficients.

## Solutions {.smaller}

```{r}
pengs <- drop_na(penguins, body_mass_g, sex, flipper_length_mm)

coef(lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = pengs))
pengs |> summarise(mean = mean(body_mass_g), .by = species)

pengs |>
  mutate(species = fct_relevel(species, "Gentoo")) |>
  lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = _) |>
  coef()
```

## Solutions {.smaller}

```{r}
pengs_sum <- pengs
contrasts(pengs_sum$species) <- contr.sum(3)
coef(lm(body_mass_g ~ species, data = pengs_sum))

coef(lm(body_mass_g ~ sex + flipper_length_mm, data = pengs))
```

. . .

Males are about `r round(coef(lm(body_mass_g ~ sex + flipper_length_mm, data = pengs))["sexmale"])` g heavier than females with the same flipper length.

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- R stores categories as [factors]{.hl}; the first level is the reference
- [Treatment coding]{.hl} compares each level with the reference; sum coding compares each with the grand mean
- `k` levels → `k − 1` coefficients; change the reference to see other comparisons
- Categorical and continuous predictors can be combined: one slope, several intercepts
:::
